humanStory.title: We saw the gap firsthand. So we packed our tablets and walked into a classroom.
humanStory.lead: This didn't begin as an NGO proposal or a corporate mandate. It began inside college hostel rooms and lab benches at NIAT, among students who were learning the most transformative technology of our time — and realized almost nobody was sharing it with the classrooms down the road.
paragraphs: Every day at NIAT, we write code, fine-tune models, and experiment with generative tools. We see where the world is racing. But when we looked outside our campus gates, we saw government school students who had only ever seen a computer used for typing tests or teacher spreadsheets.

The divide wasn't about intelligence — these kids are sharp, inquisitive, and quick to grasp ideas. The divide was pure, arbitrary access. Private schools were integrating AI copilots into 6th grade, while rural and community schools didn't have anyone to show them what an algorithm actually does.

We realized tutoring textbook physics or math was already happening. But almost no one was demystifying AI for kids who needed it most. We decided to take what we were learning inside NIAT and turn it into something we could pass forward.
progression: Decide to share what they know
humanStory.closingQuote: Learning becomes more meaningful when passed forward.

whoAreTheStudents.title: Undergraduates by day. Classroom mentors on weekends.
whoAreTheStudents.subtitle: Teach AI for India is run entirely by NIAT students across campuses in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Meet a few of the campus coordinators and volunteers bringing AI to life.

profiles.name: [VERIFY: Sneha Reddy]
profiles.story: Guides 15 campus volunteers each week. Specializes in translating machine learning fundamentals into intuitive Telugu analogies.
profiles.quote: "When a 7th grader realizes the computer responds to her thoughts, her entire posture changes."
profiles.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Sneha Reddy facilitating at ZPHS Bachupally]

profiles.name: [VERIFY: Ravi Teja]
profiles.story: Visits rural headmasters across Vizag district to schedule free workshop slots and set up mobile demonstration labs.
profiles.quote: "Headmasters are often skeptical until they see our students leave with working prompts they created themselves."
profiles.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Ravi Teja meeting with school principal]

profiles.name: [VERIFY: Karthik Mohan]
profiles.story: Manages offline cache kits and shared tablets so sessions run smoothly even in schools with zero broadband connectivity.
profiles.quote: "We carry our own mobile hotspots and battery packs. A school's lack of Wi-Fi should never stop a child from exploring AI."
profiles.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Karthik Mohan setting up tablets]

profiles.name: [VERIFY: Ananya Sharma]
profiles.story: Designs the 'Session 3: AI Safety & Ethics' module, teaching students how to spot deepfakes and identify biased outputs.
profiles.quote: "Teaching safety isn't about scaring kids — it's about making them discerning, confident digital citizens."
profiles.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Ananya Sharma explaining safety concepts on blackboard]

profiles.name: [VERIFY: Ahladini Sindhu Sri]
profiles.story: Coordinates transport and logistics to bring student volunteers into remote mandal schools across Rangareddy district.
profiles.quote: "The warmest welcomes come from the schools furthest from the city highway."
profiles.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Ahladini Sindhu Sri on campus]

profiles.name: [VERIFY: Jahnavi Chandra]
profiles.story: Pairs one-on-one with students who feel nervous around touchscreens, building their confidence prompt by prompt.
profiles.quote: "When they see an elder college sister coding and teaching, girls in the back row immediately move to the front."
profiles.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Jahnavi Chandra mentoring a student]

fromLearningToClassrooms.title: How the work actually reaches a child.

operatingLoop.name: Identify & Connect
operatingLoop.description: Student outreach leads map government schools in their district, meet with the headmaster, and secure classroom time slots.

operatingLoop.name: Prepare & Train
operatingLoop.description: Volunteers rehearse age-appropriate analogies, prepare bilingual prompt sheets in Telugu & English, and test offline demo kits.

operatingLoop.name: Enter the Classroom
operatingLoop.description: Student teams arrive with shared tablets and demo setups, guiding students through active, screen-shared experimentation.

operatingLoop.name: Listen & Document
operatingLoop.description: Every question, student artwork, and teacher reflection is logged in verified session reports with signed attendance.

operatingLoop.name: Refine & Loop
operatingLoop.description: Learnings from one classroom directly improve the next session across all 9 collegiate campus chapters.

fourSessionJourney.title: AI Awareness
fourSessionJourney.summary: What is AI, where does it live, and how is it different from normal software? Separating myth from reality through everyday analogies.
fourSessionJourney.outcome: Students understand that AI learns from examples and is built by people, not magic.

fourSessionJourney.title: AI Conversations & Prompt Engineering
fourSessionJourney.summary: Writing descriptive prompts in Telugu and English. Exploring how clarity, detail, and context shape generated images and text.
fourSessionJourney.outcome: Every student creates at least two original visual generations using their own ideas.

fourSessionJourney.title: AI Safety, Ethics & Future Careers
fourSessionJourney.summary: Spotting AI hallucinations, understanding data privacy, recognizing deepfakes, and discovering careers in tech.
fourSessionJourney.outcome: Students develop critical thinking to question AI outputs rather than believing everything on screen.

fourSessionJourney.title: Using AI for Building & Problem Solving
fourSessionJourney.summary: Students work in small teams to brainstorm how AI can solve real issues in their school, agriculture, or village health.
fourSessionJourney.outcome: Teams present their AI problem-solving concepts and receive Certificate of Completion.

whatChangesInAClassroom.title: What actually changes in a classroom?
whatChangesInAClassroom.subtitle: We convert every session feature into an observable outcome — putting the student first, before the organization.

outcomes.feature: Hands-on tablet workshops instead of blackboard lectures
outcomes.benefit: so students can touch the tools, write prompts directly, and see their own ideas materialize on screen.
outcomes.observable: Students overcome technology hesitation within the first 15 minutes.

outcomes.feature: Bilingual prompt instruction in Telugu and English
outcomes.benefit: so students can think, experiment, and create in the mother tongue they feel most natural and confident in.
outcomes.observable: Over 70% of first prompts are formulated in Telugu before students try English variations.

outcomes.feature: Practical lessons on AI hallucinations and biases
outcomes.benefit: so students can question computer outputs rather than treating digital screens as infallible sources of truth.
outcomes.observable: Students actively challenge incorrect AI answers in classroom fact-check exercises.

outcomes.benefit: so students can see relatable role models and ask honest questions about college, coding, and technology careers.
outcomes.observable: Students stay behind after the bell to ask about high-school subject streams.

outcomes.benefit: so students can discover that technology is a creative problem-solving tool for their own village or neighbourhood.
outcomes.observable: Teams propose ideas ranging from crop pest scanners to bilingual exam helpers.

outcomes.feature: Permanent printed prompt guides and student workbooks
outcomes.benefit: so students can revisit prompt structures, share concepts with siblings, and continue learning after volunteers leave.
outcomes.observable: Teachers report students referring to workbooks during subsequent computer lab hours.

storiesFromTheField.title: Three moments that shaped this movement.
storiesFromTheField.subtitle: Unrehearsed moments from actual classrooms that showed us why this work cannot wait.

stories.title: The Allu Arjun Moment
stories.quote: "Anna, can it make a picture of Allu Arjun?"
stories.narrative: The room had started silent. Thirty 7th graders sat stiffly, afraid that touching the tablets might break them. Then one student broke the ice with a grin. The NIAT volunteer didn't redirect him to a curriculum slide; he asked: 'What is he wearing? Where is he standing? What color is the sky?' In ten minutes, the entire room was shouting descriptive keywords. When the generated portrait appeared, thirty kids leaped to their feet. In that single moment, technology transformed from an intimidating machine into a canvas for their own imagination.
stories.speaker: Raju, Class 7 Student
stories.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Students celebrating an image prompt output]

stories.title: Prompts in Our Mother Tongue
stories.quote: "I thought computers only worked for people who speak fluent English."
stories.narrative: Kavitha had always felt left out during computer periods because software menus were in English. When our volunteers demonstrated that prompt models understand Telugu nuance — from describing a village harvest festival to local mythological tales — she spent thirty minutes crafting a prompt about a girl flying a kite over Telangana paddy fields. Seeing her native language command high-level machine outputs altered how she viewed her own capability.
stories.speaker: Kavitha, Class 8 Student
stories.photoSlot: [REAL PHOTO: Student taking notes in bilingual workbook]

stories.title: The Headmaster's Verdict
stories.quote: "Our children have intelligence. What they lack is exposure. You gave them exposure."
stories.narrative: Headmaster Balaji had seen many external visitors deliver one-off motivational speeches that left no lasting trace. What surprised him was seeing college students sit beside kids on benches, work through four consecutive structured sessions, and leave behind functional workbooks. 'They didn't lecture from a podium,' he said. 'They gave each child the tablet and waited patiently until the child figured it out.'
stories.speaker: Balaji, School Headmaster

items.question: Who is behind Teach AI for India?
items.answer: Teach AI for India is founded, organized, and delivered by undergraduate students at NIAT. College students form campus chapters, design bilingual session plans, coordinate with local government schools, and travel to classrooms as volunteer facilitators. Central guidance ensures child safety protocols, rigorous curriculum standards, and verified documentation across all chapters.

items.question: What is NIAT's role?
items.answer: NIAT is the learning environment and academic ecosystem where our student volunteers master advanced software, AI fundamentals, and engineering principles. Teach AI for India is what the students chose to build using that knowledge. NIAT supports the student initiative with training environments and ecosystem encouragement, but TAI is student-led and student-run.

items.question: Is this a one-time activity or a structured program?
items.answer: It is a structured program. While we offer introductory demo sessions to break the ice, partner schools participate in a structured four-session journey: 1. AI Awareness, 2. AI Conversations & Prompt Engineering, 3. AI Safety, Ethics & Future Careers, and 4. Using AI for Building & Problem Solving. Each school cohort is tracked across this progression.

items.question: Does it actually reach students in need?
items.answer: Yes. We focus specifically on government and community schools across Telangana and Andhra Pradesh where students have zero prior access to generative AI or modern digital creation tools. Every session is documented with photographs, headmaster acknowledgements, and verified student attendance counts.

items.question: How can our school, company, or institution partner with you?
items.answer: You can partner with us in multiple ways: schools can invite our campus teams for free four-session workshop cohorts; educators can provide curriculum feedback; tech companies can donate tablets or provide guest mentors; and organizations can help underwrite student workbooks or rural transport. Reach out via the conversation form below to get started.
